newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar surges versus mark and yen after G7 meeting.
newsitem.headline: Dollar surges versus mark and yen after G7 meeting.

text.p: The dollar surged on Monday after a weekend meeting of the powerful Group of Seven (G7) nations produced a surprisingly low-key statement that dealers took as a signal that the U.S. currency's rise is not over.
In its final communique after its meeting in Washington on Sunday, the group talked about the risks posed by currency volatility but failed to mention the fast-falling Japanese yen.

"The dollar started climbing after (Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi) Mitsuzuka's remarks saying that the G7 statement would not specifically refer to the yen," said Wataru Ito, deputy general manager Sanwa Bank Ltd's treasury department.
Mitsuzuka told Reuters as he emerged from the G7 meeting that the communique did not make a specific reference to recent movements in the yen.
Instead the group said that "exchange rates should reflect economic fundamentals and that excess volatility and significant deviations from fundamentals are undesirable."
Financial analysts said the statement opened the door for the dollar to climb to 130 yen, a level not seen since May 1992.
Ito said some traders had contracted to buy yen against the dollar, expecting the G7 to make a strong statement about the excessive decline in the yen.

When the statement came out, they were sent scrambling to cover their positions, helping to push the dollar up to 127.10 yen in early Tokyo trading. Later in the day it fell back to around 126.75 yen.
Traders were also surprised that the Bank of Japan did not move as the dollar surged.

The market believes the BOJ is ready to fight a rise in the dollar with massive selling in the open market but there was no market intervention seen and none of the usual signals the central bank gives that intervention might be coming.

"The BOJ (Bank of Japan) maintained utter silence despite the dollar soaring in the post-G7 market. But it may still be saving its energy for (dollar-selling) intervention and the market is fully aware of that," said Takashi Okura, chief dealer at First National Bank of Chicago.
Dealers said the dollar jumped against the German currency on comments by Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer after the G7 meeting that foreign exchange rates reflected economic fundamentals.
"All in all, I have the impression that rates are appropriate and reflect fundamentals," Tietmeyer said.

The greenback rose as high as 1.7395 marks in early trade, its highest level since February 1994, although it retreated modestly on later comments by Tietmeyer that the United States wanted a strong dollar but not a stronger dollar.

In their joint communique, the central bank governors and finance ministers of the G7, comprising Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States, also said members would cooperate as appropriate in the foreign exchange markets.
Other Japanese financial markets were little affected by the G7 meeting.
Stocks rose modestly in light trading ahead of a Tuesday holiday in Japan with the Nikkei index rising 57.51 points to close at 18,670.37.
Japanese government bonds ended slightly lower with interest primarily in better-than-expected industrial production figures.
